units: a hard surface sends a short jolt back into the foot as it lands
the jolt travels up to the ankle joint and then to the joints of the leg
the muscles soak up part of the impact, which brings tiredness on sooner
stride length shortens of its own accord on that kind of ground
the foot then lands closer to the hips
a shorter stride covers less ground and brings the pace down
the body quickens the rate of the steps to make up for it, at the cost of more breath
coaches advise alternating the surfaces trained on
repeating an identical movement on an identical surface injures more than the distance covered
text: Land on hard ground and the ground answers with a short, sharp jolt. It travels up through the ankle, then into the knee and the hip. Muscle soaks up part of it, so tiredness arrives sooner than it would on a yielding surface. The stride shortens of its own accord: the foot comes down closer to the hips, and the joint takes less strain. Pace drops as a direct result, since every step covers less ground. To make up the difference, the body quickens the turnover of the legs, and that costs more breath. Coaches therefore ask their runners to alternate the surfaces they train on. A soft one gives the tendon room to recover, while a firm one builds bone. What breaks a runner is rarely the distance covered. It is the same movement, laid down again and again on the very same surface.

units: the club coach warned that ankles would give out before breath did
ground hardened by the cold stopped the boots from gripping
half the squad was limping when the season started again
the players blamed their kit, then the man who ran the sports hall, then bad luck
a player who worked as a physiotherapist suggested a balance drill on one foot
the drill is done on a soft cushion, with no hand on the wall, before every session
the players thought the drill ridiculous at the start
the sprains grew rarer once the habit had been taken up
the routine now opens every session, whatever state the ground is in
text: Our coach kept telling us our ankles would give out long before our lungs, and he was right. The moment the cold hardened the pitch, the studs stopped biting, and half the squad was limping by the time we started again. We blamed the boots first, then the man who ran the sports hall, then plain bad luck. One of the players, a physiotherapist by trade, put a deal to us: a spell of balancing on one foot before every session, on a soft cushion, with no hand on the wall. Nobody believed a word of it. At first we laughed at ourselves, wobbling about like badly planted posts. Then the sprains thinned out, and coming back after the break stopped feeling like a sick bay. The drill opens every session now, frozen pitch, soaked pitch or dry. Our coach has yet to admit it was not his idea.

units: three families of sole stand apart at the moment of buying
the thick, soft sole damps the impact and suits long outings on the road
the thick sole wears through quickly and leaves the foot unsteady on descents
the thin sole brings the foot nearer the ground and passes the push on better
the thin sole leaves the tendon exposed to repeated jarring
the studded sole is meant for soft ground and turns uncomfortable on a hard track
it is worth trying models on once the foot has already swollen
one should jog on a firm surface before completing the purchase
how well the joint is held is tested by turning on the spot
text: Buying a sports shoe comes down to weighing up three families of sole, say the assistants trained to advise on them. The first is thick and soft: it damps the impact and suits long outings on tarmac, but it wears through quickly and leaves the foot unsteady on a descent. The second is thinner. It brings the foot nearer the ground and passes the push on more faithfully, though it leaves the tendon open to repeated jarring. The third carries studs and belongs on soft ground; on a hard track it turns noisy and awkward. The method itself holds no mystery. Try the models on once the foot has swollen after a long walk. Jog on a firm surface before you reach for your card. Then turn on the spot to compare how each one holds the ankle. A shoe that suits you draws less notice than one that rubs.

units: the sports hall reopens after its fittings were put back in order
the tumbling track has been laid again from scratch
a springboard stands in front of the vaulting table
the bars carry the trace of the chalk left there by those who train
the hanging rings serve mostly for strength work in the upper body
a pit filled with foam blocks catches the falls of those learning
beginners turn up at the end of the evening
attendance has risen since the reopening
those who run the place put the rise down to the renewal of the apparatus
text: A smell of varnish still hangs over the mats in the hall that has just been put back in order. The tumbling track, laid again from scratch, gives out a dull note under the visitors' shoes. Then comes the springboard, a curved plank set before the vaulting table, which jumpers test with the heel before trusting themselves to it. Further on, the bars carry the white trace that every gymnast leaves behind in chalk. The rings hang from the ceiling on long cables and serve mostly for strength work in the upper body. At the far end, a pit filled with foam blocks catches the falls of those still learning, and the soft thud of it keeps time through the evening. Beginners come late on, when the room still belongs to the quiet. Attendance has climbed since the reopening, and the people who run the place put that down to the renewal of the apparatus.

units: the run-up settles the speed at which the board is reached
the jumper builds speed gradually, keeping the chest upright
the second to last contact serves to drop the centre of gravity
the last contact with the ground lasts less time than the ones before it
that last contact turns forward speed into a drive upwards
the board bends under the load and then hands back the energy it has stored
the arms rise at the moment the board sends the jumper away
rotation starts during the climb and not after the highest point
a landing that is too stiff passes the shock into the joint of the foot
text: It all starts with the run-up, whose length settles the speed at which the board is reached. The jumper builds that speed gradually, chest upright, stride even. On the second to last contact he drops his centre of gravity, bending the supporting leg further. The last contact with the ground lasts less time than any before it, and it is the one that turns forward speed into lift. The board bends under the load, then hands back the energy it has stored. The arms rise at that exact moment; otherwise the drive leaks away. Rotation starts during the climb, never after the highest point of the flight. The landing is taken on both feet, knees bent, chest a little forward. A landing that is too stiff sends the shock straight into the ankle and the tendon, which accounts for most of the injuries seen at this stage.

units: nothing obliges a child to settle on one discipline before adolescence
early specialisation loads the same movements onto the same joints
that loading brings on tendon overload before growth has finished
a narrow range of movement makes adapting hard when the ground changes
weariness is given as the chief reason for giving up
clubs push towards specialisation because early results draw funding
the writer proposes delaying selection in the junior ranks
he recommends requiring a second activity of every competitor
text: Nothing obliges a child to settle on one discipline before adolescence, and yet the clubs press for it, with effects that can be measured. Early specialisation loads the same movements onto the same joints, so overload of the tendon shows up before growth has finished. It also thins out the range of movement a young athlete owns: a teenager who has known one apparatus, or one way of landing, adapts badly the moment the ground changes. Then comes weariness, the chief reason for giving up somewhere between late childhood and adulthood. If clubs hold to their course, it is because results won early draw funding. We would do better to delay selection in the junior ranks and to ask a second activity of every competitor. A sporting life is built on the variety of the movements met, not on their repetition.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)

she brought in a build-up spread over three weeks

text: The club calls her its strength coach, and her whole office fits into a kit bag left on the tiles at the edge of the pool. She swam in competition when she was young, until the evening a tendon gave way and brought that career to a halt there and then. She went back to studying, then came back to the poolside with a question in mind. Watching her athletes, she noticed that injuries seldom struck in the thick of the season: they came on the return, after a break. So she brought in a return to training spread over three weeks, built from light loads and movements deliberately slowed down. Heavy weights enter only at the end of it, once the ankle and the shoulder have their range back. The number of injuries has fallen since, and clubs nearby have taken up the same method.

units: the writer used two gyms over the same season
the first gym is fitted with guided machines and screens
guided machines force a fixed path on the movement
the second gym sits in a badly heated shed
the second gym offers mostly bars, free weights and apparatus
the coach at the second gym corrects your position without being asked
the writer made more progress in the less comfortable gym
he still recommends the smart gym to anyone the weights frighten
text: I used two gyms over the same season, and they have almost nothing in common. The first one gleams: guided machines, screens on every wall, soft music, carpet that swallows the sound of the weights. It is a pleasant place to be, except that the machine settles the path of the movement for you, and the shoulder never learns to hold itself. The second sits in a badly heated shed, with bars, free weights and a couple of frames that creak. The floor bangs, people talk loudly, and the coach comes over to correct your position without being asked. Guess where I made progress. In the shed, of course, because a whole movement is worth more than one that is steered for you. Even so, I would send anyone the weights frighten to the smart gym: a machine that reassures beats giving up within a week.

units: the writer of the message reports to her reader on the club she has joined

the writer invites her reader to come along one evening early in the week
text: Dear neighbour, you asked me for an account of the club I have joined, so here it is. Sessions in the adult section run an hour and a half, and the first third of that goes on warming up, which took me aback at first and won me over afterwards. The equipment is sound: thick mats, a springboard in good order, and two sets of weights, from the lightest to the heaviest. The membership fee covers the loan of studded boots, worth knowing if you would rather not buy anything before you are sure. Two volunteers and one paid member of staff look after us; she is the one who follows the injured, a twisted ankle, an angry tendon. Newcomers sit in on two sessions before paying a thing. Come along one evening early in the week, the hall is quiet then and I will introduce you to the whole group.

units: the first question is about what happens on the approach to the wall
the swimmer judges the distance left without lifting the head
she adjusts the reach of her arm strokes to arrive at the right spacing
the somersault begins with the chest tipping towards the bottom
the feet come to rest against the wall, set about hip width apart
the push off the wall gives a speed higher than that of swimming
the tucked position underwater holds on to that speed
swimming has to start again before the speed falls away
a foot placed badly costs more than a length swum badly
text: What happens to a swimmer in the second before the wall? Without lifting the head, she reads off how much water she has left before the wall, and she adjusts the reach of her arms so as to arrive neither cramped nor short. And what comes next? The chest tips towards the bottom, the somersault takes hold at once, and the feet come to rest against the wall, set about hip width apart. Does that turn really count for as much as people claim it does? It does, because the push off the wall sends her away faster than she will ever swim. The tucked position underwater holds on to that speed, so long as nothing sticks out to catch the water. When should she start swimming again? Just before the speed falls away. A foot badly placed on the wall costs more than a whole length swum badly.
